Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 3 of 10): The First Global War, 1756–1783

Summary: In under thirty years Britain won Canada, became the real power in Bengal, and then lost its thirteen American colonies. This post follows the Seven Years' War, Plassey and Buxar, the Bengal famine, and the American Revolution, and shows how wars in India, the Caribbean, Europe and North America were fought in the same years and often by the same people.

---

## The big picture

The Seven Years' War (1756–1763) is sometimes called the first true world war. Britain and France fought in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines. Britain won almost everywhere, and the peace of 1763 left it with the largest empire in the world.

The victory created the problem that followed. The war doubled the national debt. London decided the American colonies should help pay for their own defence, and the colonists disagreed. Twenty years later the thirteen colonies were gone. In the same years, a private company was turning itself into the government of Bengal, one of the richest regions on earth.

## Main timeline: the Seven Years' War (1756–1763)

| Year | Where | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| 1756 | Europe | War formally declared between Britain and France |
| 1756 | Bengal | Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah takes Calcutta; the "Black Hole" incident, in which British prisoners died in a cell overnight (the numbers in the famous account by Holwell are disputed) |
| 1757 | Bengal | **Battle of Plassey (23 June).** Clive wins mainly by arranging the betrayal of the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar, who is made the new Nawab |
| 1758 | North America and West Africa | Louisbourg taken; French slave-trading posts in Senegal (Saint-Louis, Gorée) captured |
| 1759 | Many fronts | "Annus mirabilis": Quebec falls after the Battle of the Plains of Abraham (13 September), Guadeloupe taken, Minden in Germany, Lagos and Quiberon Bay at sea |
| 1760 | India and Canada | Wandiwash ends French power in south India; Montreal surrenders |
| 1761 | India | Pondicherry falls to the British |
| 1762 | Caribbean and Asia | British take Havana from Spain and Manila from Spain, plus Martinique |
| 1763 | Global | **Treaty of Paris.** Britain gets Canada, Florida, Dominica, Grenada, St Vincent, Tobago and Senegal. Havana and Manila are handed back |

## Main timeline: from trading company to ruler (1763–1784)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1763 | Royal Proclamation bans colonial settlement west of the Appalachians | Meant to calm Indigenous nations after Pontiac's War; colonists resent it |
| 1764 | **Battle of Buxar** | The Company defeats the combined forces of the Nawab of Bengal, the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II |
| 1765 | Treaty of Allahabad: the Mughal Emperor grants the EIC the **Diwani** (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa | A company now collects the taxes of tens of millions of people |
| 1765 | Stamp Act passed, repealed in 1766 | "No taxation without representation" |
| 1767 | Townshend duties | Further protest and boycotts |
| 1767–1769 | First Anglo-Mysore War against Hyder Ali | Mysore wins; the Company has to accept his terms near Madras |
| 1769–1770 | **Great Bengal Famine** | Perhaps a third of Bengal's population dies; Company revenue collection continued during it |
| 1770 | Boston Massacre; Captain Cook charts Australia's east coast and claims it | The same year as the Bengal famine |
| 1772 | Somerset v Stewart | Lord Mansfield rules an enslaved man cannot be forcibly removed from England; widely (but not quite accurately) read as abolishing slavery in England |
| 1773 | Tea Act and Boston Tea Party; Regulating Act for India | The Tea Act was partly designed to save the nearly bankrupt EIC, so the two events are linked |
| 1774 | Quebec Act; Warren Hastings becomes first Governor-General of Bengal | The Quebec Act tolerates Catholicism in Canada, which angers Protestant colonists |
| 1775 | Fighting begins at Lexington and Concord (19 April) | American War of Independence |
| 1775–1782 | First Anglo-Maratha War | Ends in a stalemate at the Treaty of Salbai |
| 1776 | Declaration of Independence; Adam Smith publishes *The Wealth of Nations* | Smith criticised both colonial monopolies and the EIC |
| 1777 | British army surrenders at Saratoga | France enters the war in 1778, Spain in 1779, the Dutch in 1780 |
| 1779 | Cook killed in Hawaii | |
| 1780 | Gordon Riots in London; Hyder Ali crushes a Company army at Pollilur | Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780–1784) begins; at Pollilur, British prisoners were taken to Seringapatam |
| 1781 | **Yorktown** (October); the Zong massacre | The Zong crew threw over 130 enslaved Africans overboard to claim insurance; the 1783 court case fuels abolitionism |
| 1782 | Battle of the Saintes; Irish "legislative independence" | Britain saves Jamaica at sea; Ireland's parliament gains more autonomy |
| 1783 | **Treaty of Paris** recognises the United States | Britain keeps Canada, Gibraltar (after a long siege) and most Caribbean islands |
| 1784 | Treaty of Mangalore with Mysore; Pitt's India Act | The British state starts formally supervising the Company |

## Meanwhile: the rest of the world (1756–1784)

| Years | Event | Region |
|---|---|---|
| 1757 | Qing China restricts European trade to Canton (the Canton System) | China, the same year as Plassey |
| 1761 | Third Battle of Panipat: Afghan Durrani forces crush the Marathas | India. The defeat weakened the Marathas just as the British were rising |
| 1762 | Catherine the Great comes to power | Russia |
| 1767 | Burmese armies sack Ayutthaya, ending the Siamese kingdom | Southeast Asia |
| 1768–1774 | Russo-Turkish War | Eastern Europe |
| 1769 | James Watt's steam engine patent | Britain, the same year the Bengal famine began |
| 1772 | First Partition of Poland | Europe |
| 1773–1775 | Pugachev's Rebellion | Russia, at the same time as the Boston Tea Party |
| 1780–1783 | Túpac Amaru II rebellion | Spanish Peru, the same years as the American war |
| 1782 | Rama I founds the Chakri dynasty and makes Bangkok the capital | Siam |
| 1783 | Laki volcanic eruption | Iceland; causes crop failures and deaths across Europe |

## Resistance: wars against British power

| Years | Who | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1756–1757 | Siraj ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal | Bengal | Defeated at Plassey and killed |
| 1760 | **Tacky's Revolt** | Jamaica | The biggest slave revolt in the 18th-century British Caribbean; it took about a year to suppress |
| 1763–1766 | **Pontiac's War** | Great Lakes region | Indigenous nations take many British forts; leads to the Proclamation Line. Includes the attempt at Fort Pitt to spread smallpox using blankets |
| 1764 | Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula, Shah Alam II | Bihar | Defeated at Buxar |
| 1767–1784 | Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore | South India | Two wars; Mysore holds its own |
| 1769–1773 | First Carib War | St Vincent | Garifuna (Black Carib) resistance forces a treaty |
| 1775–1783 | The American Revolution | Thirteen colonies | Independence |
| 1775–1782 | The Marathas | Western India | Stalemate |
| 1781 | Raja Chait Singh of Benares | Benares | Rises against Hastings's demands for money; defeated |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **1757.** Plassey happened in the same year that Qing China confined European traders to Canton. The British were gaining their power base in Bengal while being shut out of China on Chinese terms. Bengal opium would later be the tool used to break those terms.
- **1770.** In the same year the Bengal famine was killing millions, Cook reached Botany Bay and British soldiers shot five people in Boston. The Boston Massacre became a founding story; the Bengal famine is barely known in the West.
- **1773.** The Boston Tea Party and India's Regulating Act were two responses to the same crisis: the near-bankruptcy of the East India Company.
- **1775–1782.** The first Anglo-Maratha War was being fought for almost exactly the same years as the American Revolution. Britain was at war on two continents against two independent powers, and lost one of them.
- **1780.** London was burning in the Gordon Riots, the Spanish were fighting Túpac Amaru in Peru, and Hyder Ali was destroying a Company army in south India, all in the same year.

## Sources and flags

- Fred Anderson, *Crucible of War: The Seven Years' War and the Fate of Empire in British North America* (2000).
- William Dalrymple, *The Anarchy* (2019), on Plassey, Buxar, the Diwani and the 1770 famine.
- P. J. Marshall, *The Making and Unmaking of Empires: Britain, India, and America c.1750–1783* (2005), which treats the American and Indian stories together.
- Rajat Datta, *Society, Economy and the Market: Commercialization in Rural Bengal c.1760–1800* (2000), on the 1770 famine.
- Vincent Brown, *Tacky's Revolt: The Story of an Atlantic Slave War* (2020).
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Seven Years' War": https://www.britannica.com/event/Seven-Years-War
- **Flag:** The Bengal famine death toll is uncertain. "About a third of the population", sometimes stated as up to 10 million, comes from Warren Hastings's own estimate, and some modern historians argue it is too high. The Black Hole death toll (Holwell claimed 123 of 146 died) is disputed and may be heavily exaggerated. The smallpox blanket incident at Fort Pitt (1763) is documented, but whether it actually caused the outbreak among local nations is not established.
